title: Vilas Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Vilas wells have a 300 ft median depth; drilling and a finished well typically cost $10,500-$28,500.
h1: Vilas, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land near Vilas means looking past the promise of “good water” and checking the local well record. Within 5 miles, Colorado DWR records show 299 permitted wells, but only 61 are recorded as constructed. Depth is reported for 181 wells, yield for 77, and static water level for 8, so the numbers are useful but not complete for every parcel.

This area is plains country, with alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. The records include irrigation, stock, domestic, and monitoring wells, so a large reported yield does not automatically describe a household well. Use nearby permits, the intended use, and a site-specific driller’s estimate together.

sections.heading: Vilas well depths: plan around 300 feet
sections.html:
The median recorded well depth near Vilas is 300 feet. The middle half runs from 260 to 345 feet, which is the most useful range when asking a driller for an early budget. A 300-foot estimate is not a promise, but it gives a practical starting point for a typical bid in this area.

Depths vary substantially. Forty-four percent of reported wells are 100-300 feet, while 48% are 300-600 feet. Eight percent reach 600 feet or more, and the deepest record is 2,340 feet. The mix reflects different uses and locations, including irrigation wells and wells in alluvium or sedimentary rock. Before buying, compare permits near the exact lot, not just the Vilas-wide median.

sections.heading: High reported yields need the right interpretation
sections.html:
Among the 77 wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 800.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 600.0 to 1,000.0 gallons per minute. Ninety-seven percent of those reported yields are 15+ gallons per minute. No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute or in the 1-5 gallon-per-minute range, and 3% are in the 5-15 range.

Those figures are dominated by the area’s use mix: 74% of permits are for irrigation, compared with 10% domestic or household and 12% stock. Do not treat an irrigation yield as a guaranteed household supply. A new exempt household-use well has a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit, and its permitted use still matters.

sections.heading: The limited water-level record near Vilas
sections.html:
Only 8 wells report a static water level, so the local water-level sample is thin. In those records, the median depth to water is 225 feet, with the middle half from 134 to 290 feet. That is a planning reference for pump setting and construction, not a dependable prediction for an untested parcel.

The supplied records do not provide a water-level series by decade, so they do not establish that the water table is dropping or stable. A driller should evaluate the formation and nearby completed wells at the proposed location. Ask for the static level after the well rests, because pumping conditions and a static measurement answer different questions.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers showing up around Vilas
sections.html:
Permit activity is concentrated in the older record. The DWR list shows 23 permits from the 1950s, 102 from the 1960s, 32 from the 1970s, 7 from the 1980s, 6 from the 1990s, 25 from the 2000s, 28 from the 2010s, and 12 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2024, so this is not only a historical dataset.

The most active named drillers in these records are Ralph'S Welding (Woods, Ralph R), with 17 wells; S. E. Camp Drilling (Camp, S E), with 14; and Great Plains Drilling (Tweedy, Willis E), with 12. Permit history helps identify local experience, but confirm current licensing, availability, casing, grout, testing, and final construction details before hiring.

sections.heading: What a new well may cost in Vilas
sections.html:
For Vilas ground described as alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling rate model is $35-$55 per foot. At the 300-foot median depth, the drilled hole comes to about $10,500-$16,500. That is the hole only, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $16,500-$28,500 at that median depth. A 345-foot well, a 600-foot well, difficult access, extra casing, or an unexpected formation can move the price higher. Ask each bidder to separate drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, electrical, trenching, testing, and any permit-related work so competing bids describe the same scope.

sections.heading: Checks beyond depth: water quality, yield, and the lot
sections.html:
Mapped environmental records within about 10 miles include 9 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. There are 0 historic mine features in that mapped search. These records do not prove a problem on a particular parcel, but they are a reason to check the property and test the finished well for contaminants relevant to the site.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible even where nearby records look strong, especially because permits name unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer conditions in 140 wells. Cheyenne appears on 62 permits and Dakota on 50; Denver Basin aquifer wells are 0%. Confirm septic setbacks, building envelopes, access for a rig, trench routes, and the intended household use before committing to a lot.

sections.heading: A practical buying plan for Vilas and nearby plains communities
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel and pull neighboring permits, construction records, reported depths, yields, and water levels. Compare the property with records toward Walsh, 9 miles away, Springfield, 10 miles away, and Two Buttes, 13 miles away only as wider context; the closest wells usually deserve the most attention. Records near Campo, Pritchett, and Granada can show broader regional conditions but should not replace local verification.

For a build, have a licensed Colorado driller review the proposed well location before finalizing the house site. Confirm whether the permit is domestic, stock, or irrigation, and ask how the plan handles casing, grout, pump sizing, storage, electrical, and testing. If the basin is over-appropriated, ask Colorado DWR about augmentation requirements before assuming a new use is available.

faq.q: How deep are wells near Vilas, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded depth within 5 miles of Vilas is 300 feet. The middle half runs from 260 to 345 feet. Forty-four percent are 100-300 feet and 48% are 300-600 feet. Eight percent reach 600 feet or more, while the deepest record is 2,340 feet. Nearby permits are more useful than the median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Vilas?
faq.a: The local cost model is $35-$55 per foot for alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 300-foot median depth, drilling the hole is about $10,500-$16,500. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is about $16,500-$28,500. Actual bids can change with depth, access, casing, formation, and equipment choices.

faq.q: How much water do wells near Vilas produce?
faq.a: Of the 77 wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 800.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 600.0-1,000.0 gallons per minute. Ninety-seven percent report 15+ gallons per minute. Most permits are irrigation wells, however, so these figures should not be applied directly to a household well without a site-specific test and review.

faq.q: Is well water near Vilas safe to drink?
faq.a: The records alone cannot establish that water is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, mapped records include 9 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test a completed household well for appropriate contaminants, especially after construction, and review nearby environmental records rather than relying on a neighboring well’s reported yield.

faq.q: What should I check before buying land near Vilas with a well?
faq.a: Check the exact permit, intended use, construction status, depth, yield, static water level, and nearby wells. Only 61 of 299 permitted wells are recorded as constructed, while 181 report depth, 77 yield, and 8 static level. Also confirm septic and building setbacks, rig access, electrical and trench routes, and any augmentation requirement for the proposed use.
